fish-tank-2009.gazette: Katie Jarvis was cast off a railway platform in Tilbury, mid-argument with her boyfriend, having never acted. The shoot stayed on a working Essex council estate — handheld, boxy Academy frame, script pages handed out as the schedule advanced rather than in advance. Cannes gave it the Jury Prize that May.

the-kid-with-a-bike-2011.gazette: The Dardennes have shot the same industrial belt around Liège since the mid-1990s, mixing newcomers with professionals and following them at shoulder height. Their films normally carry no music at all; this one breaks for a few bars of Beethoven, then goes back to traffic and footsteps. It shared the Grand Prix at Cannes.

tomboy-2011.gazette: Sciamma shot in a suburban housing development across a few summer weeks, on a small digital camera, with children who had never acted. Games were allowed to run as games — rules negotiated on the spot, dialogue arriving as the kids arrived at it. Two years later, screenings arranged for French schools drew an organized protest campaign.
tomboy-2011.prism: Ten-year-olds can't consent to what a film will mean to strangers a decade on. The naturalism that makes it feel true is borrowed from them, and they're the ones carrying it afterward.

wuthering-heights-2011.gazette: Academy ratio, available light, a cast from outside the profession: Arnold took her council-estate method onto the Yorkshire moors. There is no score and no sound that wasn't already in the field — wind, rain, boots in mud, animals. Heathcliff was played by a Black actor, a reading the novel's own description permits and screen adaptations had spent a century declining.

girlhood-2014.gazette: The four leads were found through street casting in Paris, none of them actors, and the film was built around the estates and shopping malls they already moved through. A Rihanna single was licensed so one hotel-room scene could play out whole, without a cut away. It runs nearly the length of the track.

two-days-one-night-2014.gazette: The setup is a vote: a factory's workers choose between a colleague's job and their own bonus, canvassed one doorstep at a time over a weekend. The Dardennes built the film around an international star for the first time, then shot her as they shoot everyone — handheld, long takes, repeated until the performance wears off. The factory makes solar panels.
two-days-one-night-2014.prism: Precarity runs smoothest when the workers administer it themselves; management never has to say no, the colleagues do. That delegation is the realism here, more than the handheld camera is.

happy-hour-2015.gazette: Hamaguchi assembled his cast from an acting workshop he ran in Kobe for people with no professional experience. The finished film runs past five hours and gives its set pieces — a balance workshop, a public reading, an argument that refuses to resolve — close to their real duration. The four leads shared the acting prize at Locarno.

ixcanul-2015.gazette: Bustamante shot on the flanks of an active volcano with a cast of Kaqchikel Maya who had not acted, in a language that had effectively never carried a feature. The camera mostly holds still and wide while labor takes its own time: coffee plants, pigs, the mountain smoking behind the frame. Berlin sent it home with a Silver Bear.

american-honey-2016.gazette: The lead was found on a Florida beach during spring break, one of a cast picked out of parking lots and street corners across the country. Shooting followed the story's own route in sequence, Oklahoma up through the Dakotas, cast and crew traveling it together. Arnold kept the Academy frame, so the horizon stays cropped for the entire trip.
american-honey-2016.prism: Street casting gets you faces the industry can't manufacture, and it also means the realism is subsidized by people with no career to protect if the thing goes wrong. Arnold is candid about the road and quiet about that arrangement.

divines-2016.gazette: Benyamina had already founded an association to move young people from the estates into film work, and she cast largely out of it. The locations are a shantytown on the edge of a Paris suburb and the blocks beside it, filmed in place rather than rebuilt. Cannes gave it the Caméra d'Or, the prize reserved for a first feature.

a-gentle-creature-2017.gazette: Loznitsa came to fiction from documentary, and he shoots the queue outside a Russian prison the way he shoots archive crowds: static, wide, everyone in focus at once. The plot is a single errand — a parcel to an imprisoned husband, returned to sender, a woman traveling to find out why — routed through trains, waiting rooms and offices that explain nothing. Most of the faces come from outside the profession, held long enough to be catalogued.

beach-rats-2017.gazette: Hittman shot Gerritsen Beach on 16mm, close in and mostly at the ends of the day, with a supporting crew of young men drawn from the neighborhood itself. The lead was a British unknown who turned up with the accent and no track record. Sundance gave it the directing award; it opened that August, the season it takes place in.
beach-rats-2017.prism: Grain and shallow focus read as intimacy, but they're also a way of shooting a closeted kid without ever quite showing him. The texture and the subject are running the same evasion.

the-florida-project-2017.gazette: Baker shot at working budget motels on the highway strip outside Orlando, a few miles from the Disney gates, among residents paying by the week. The mother was cast off Instagram with no acting experience; the one established professional in the film plays the motel manager. The final scene was shot on a phone, without permits, inside the park.

ayka-2018.gazette: Dvortsevoy spent years on the shoot, partly because he wanted real Moscow blizzards and had to wait out winters that would not supply them. He came from documentary and kept its terms: extended takes at arm's length from a Kyrgyz migrant with a debt and a newborn, sound limited to what the street and the basement workrooms produce. His lead took the acting prize at Cannes.

lean-on-pete-2018.gazette: Haigh filmed the racing at a working Portland track on the cheap end of the circuit, where horses change hands quickly and get moved on faster. From there the film heads east across Oregon into the high desert with a teenager and a quarter horse, declining nearly every consolation the setup offers. Adapted from Willy Vlautin's novel, it keeps the book's flat register: things get worse, and no one on screen treats that as remarkable.
lean-on-pete-2018.prism: A boy-and-his-horse road movie comes pre-loaded with a redemption arc, and Haigh spends the runtime refusing to cash it. What's left is arithmetic: every way out costs money the kid doesn't have.
